Abstract This study examines the criteria for participant selection in the Smart Sawah Berskala Besar Asnaf (SSBBA) program administered by the Kedah State Zakat Board, aimed at facilitating economic growth for the asnaf (needy) group. It outlines human capital characteristics grounded on Islamic principles, which promote sustainable socio-economic development among those considered marginalized. This study employs a qualitative technique to analyse secondary sources, including Islamic scholarship and literature on human capital. Through the analysis of data from reports and previously conducted studies, it offers an extensive overview of the Kedah State Zakat Board’s (LZNK) selection procedure within the Zon Pembangunan Ekonomi Ummah (ZPEU) framework, emphasizing participant characteristics conducive to economic empowerment. These findings underscore selection criteria that prioritise ethics, resilience, and practical skills, which are consistent with Islamic principles and contribute to the objectives of the ZPEU. The research emphasizes the significance of a self-sustaining socio-economic ecosystem that enables asnaf beneficiaries to evolve from receivers to independent contributors, fostering innovation in community development. This study amalgamates Islamic principles with structured human capital management, presenting a distinctive methodology for participant selection. LZNK’s concept illustrates the synergy between ancient Islamic beliefs and contemporary human capital methods in augmenting marginalized communities and establishing a support structure that promotes ethically and economically sustainable community development. Keywords: Lembaga Zakat, participant selection, case study, Malaysia 1. Introduction Management in Islam emphasizes quality work management and the planned development of human capital. In Malaysia, where the majority are from the Bottom 40% (B40 group), including asnaf (the needy) and the poor, it is appropriate for the government to provide an economic development plan, especially for this target group (Ravi & Redzuan, 2022). The Kedah State Zakat Board (LZNK) has spearheaded a project called the Zon Pembangunan Ekonomi Ummah (ZPEU), which began in Yan and has now expanded to Alor Star, Kubang Pasu, and Kuala Muda in Kedah. In Islam, the effectiveness of a program is holistic, comprehensive, and aimed at achieving al-falah (success) for the development of a civilized ummah (community) (Omar & Khairi, 2024). Perhaps no other function contributes more to an organization's success than the process of recruiting and selecting participants. Recruitment is the process of attracting suitable candidates to apply for any job vacancies or positions and selecting the most appropriate candidates from the applicants (Krasna et al., 2023). This is because human capital management and development are key components that must be emphasized in driving and advancing an organization. Good organizational management emphasizes the structured and dynamic development and management of human capital. A well-organized organization is typically achieved when it wisely manages itself to ensure alignment with management functions in developing the organization’s resources and assets toward quality products and services. According to Dubey et al. (2023), good management also stresses the importance of positive relationships between management and subordinates, which should be characterized by tolerance, cooperation, and mutual assistance in advancing effective organizational management. Therefore, discrimination should be avoided in human capital management to ensure high-quality and respected management. Human capital must have a clear sense of purpose and direction in life, be bound by religious principles, possess noble life philosophies, uphold ethics and integrity, and have strong mental fortitude (Hossain, 2023). This includes the ability to reject any negative influences, along with the capability to make accurate, swift, and optimistic decisions (Sanad, 2024). Kankaew (2021) stated that individuals who are talented, confident, knowledgeable, ethical, progressive, disciplined, innovative, creative, competitive, and possess high moral values constitute human capital. Therefore, human capital development is a process aimed at nurturing a pious soul. This is because a lack of piety can negatively affect the proper Multidiscip. Sci. J. Hence, research into the selection criteria for participants in the ‘Smart Sawah Berskala Besar Asnaf’ (SBBA) program is essential to ensure that the ZPEU initiative achieves the goals set by LZNK. The concept of economic development from an Islamic perspective is outlined in the Quran, further clarified in the hadith, and continues to be discussed by scholars and jurists, as economic development is a broad and crucial issue for governance (Chapra, 2016). Economic development from an Islamic viewpoint is the holistic development of individuals, encompassing four main aspects: environmental, physical, spiritual, and socio-cultural development (Al-Jayyousi et al., 2022). The primary factor in development is the human being itself, which can be divided into several dimensions such as capital, labor, organization, education, skills, attitude, and incentives. Therefore, the ZPEU program by LZNK has outlined four main objectives: (i) To create employment opportunities for the asnaf; (ii) To establish a new economic ecosystem for the ummah; (iii) To create a socio-economic cycle of "From Asnaf to Asnaf". This study has several characteristics, making it unique to get it published. First of all, this is first study that is using zakat as instrument to regulate poverty in the agriculture sector of Peninsular Malaysia. While previous literature on zakat is mostly focused on testing Zakat as minimizing poverty while this study is focusing on how Zakat can help community to become a productive member of society by using land assigned by LZNK to earn their living and raising their standards of life. Study also added valuable contribution in the context of system model in Malaysian context. Further, this study is providing a way forward to the policy makers to know the real picture of population under study which they will use for policy making purpose. 2. Theoretical support Human Capital Theory (HCT) by Becker provides a reasonable grounding for this study. HCT underscores the significance of education, skills, and training in improving individual productivity and economic welfare (Abdou, 2023). The SSBBA program is congruent with HCT by offering participants agricultural training, financial literacy, and technical skills, hence enhancing their socio-economic standing. The program promotes self-sufficiency and enduring economic sustainability by providing asnaf with key competences (Schultz, 1961). This study is also supported by Islamic Economic Theory by Chapra (1992) by incorporating Islamic principles into economic empowerment and the distribution of zakat. This paradigm emphasises justice, equality, and the optimal utilisation of resources to attain socio-economic equilibrium (Rahim & Mohammed, 2018). The SSBBA program embodies these ideals by guaranteeing equitable resource allocation, fostering ethical economic practices, and enabling asnaf to evolve from recipients to contributors. The program's systematic methodology corresponds with the Islamic principle of Al-Falah (holistic success), bolstering sustained socio-economic growth (Ahmed, 2004). The amalgamation of Human Capital Theory and Islamic Economic Theory provides a robust theoretical framework for comprehending how systematic human capital investment and faith-oriented economic models facilitate poverty reduction and empowerment in marginalised areas. 3. Literature Review Zakat in the Muslim economics is described as supplementary support, in addition to government support, for the financial needs of the impoverished and needy. Zakat is a mandatory responsibility for Muslims to allocate 2.5% of their money to an authorised religious institution (Siregar et al., 2023). The collected zakat will thereafter be allocated to eight categories of eligible asnaf. The roster of qualifying asnaf comprises: “impoverished, needy, amil, muallaf, al-Gharimin, fisabilillah, and Ibnussabil”, with particular emphasis often placed on the first two categories (Zulkifli et al., 2021). Consequently, zakat is often seen as the most effective instrument within an Islamic economic system to help alleviating poverty and promoting economic prosperity. Nonetheless, the significance of zakat in poverty alleviation is sometimes undervalued. The primary discourse around zakat often focusses on the inadequacies of zakat institutions in effectively handling zakat funds (Zulkifli et al., 2021). The potential of zakat to harmonise the Muslim economy remains untapped due to the prevailing attitudes towards zakat institutions. This study seeks to elucidate the underexamined function of zakat as a mechanism for poverty alleviation, particularly within the Muslim world, focusing on its potential to mitigate poverty in the context of Malaysia. Poverty is a widespread issue across worldwide. Following this the United Nations' 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development delineates 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with the foremost objective being the eradication of poverty, encapsulated by the slogan “End poverty in all its forms everywhere,” underscoring the gravity with which this issue is approached on the global stage. This issue has been repeatedly posed in several research, with diverse responses (Majeed et al., 2025; Wang & Peng, 2023). Poverty is seen as inadequate money or resources to fulfil fundamental demands within a global framework (Lister, 2021). Discussions on poverty have been shaped by the need to discern the appropriate methods for addressing poverty- related difficulties, as well as to comprehend the causative factors and consequences of poverty itself. The definition of poverty https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Majid et al. (2026) 3 has evolved throughout the years, including income, fundamental requirements, and capacities (Bray et al., 2020). One is considered impoverished if, and only if, one's income falls below the established poverty threshold. Numerous countries, guided by World Bank indicators, have established income poverty thresholds to assess advancements in poverty reduction (Ravallion & Chen, 2019). The poverty threshold is sometimes delineated by the money required to secure a certain quantity of food (Gundersen, 2021). Muslim countries are using Zakat for poverty eradication. The significance of Zakat in poverty alleviation is attributed to Al-Qaradawi, who in 1993 highlighted its potential to emancipate the Muslim community from the turmoil of poverty (Zulkifli et al., 2021). Mohd Sabri later in 1997 extended the conversation, highlighting the capacity of zakat to redistribute wealth and re-establish social equilibrium within society (Zulkifli et al., 2021). Zakat serves as a fundamental element in establishing a robust Islamic society, especially regarding the socio-economic condition of the ummah (Bin-Nashwan et al., 2020). The efficacy of zakat as a mechanism for poverty alleviation has been established for some time, as the distribution methods employed can fulfil the needs of asnaf, whether through regular assistance or capital support to foster their independence (Aziz et al., 2020). Zakat help may be used as capital to establish a company, so supporting the economy of the impoverished (Harun & Ab Rahman, 2021; Meerangani, 2019). Furthermore, seed fund support may serve as company capital and provide exposure to enhance the income of the impoverished (Anis & Kassim, 2016). Consequently, zakat not only alleviates poverty but also fosters social and ethical values throughout communities to attain sustainable development. Khamis et al. (2024) demonstrates that the allocation of zakat to asnaf has effectively mitigated income distribution disparities. Likewise, research (Ali et al., 2015; Marwan, 2022; Yamaludin et al., 2024) has shown the function of zakat in alleviating poverty, redistributing income, and fostering wealth equality within Islam. Zakat effectively mitigates income distribution disparities and successfully addresses the issue of poverty. Sari et al. (2024) discovered that zakat assistance significantly influenced quality of life. This research reveals that the impoverished may enhance their quality of life via children's education funded by zakat assistance. The logistic regression findings indicate the correlation between zakat assistance and five quality of life indicators. Mat Daud and Wahid (2024) revealed that Zakat assistance substantially influences educational quality and the social engagement of impoverished individuals. From an Islamic viewpoint, the essential function of zakat in alleviating poverty should be emphasized to guarantee that every qualified Muslim may take use of this opportunity. The authority responsible for zakat administration must engage in comprehensive planning to ensure that zakat money effectively support long-term programs aimed at improving the lives of the impoverished and disadvantaged (Mat Daud & Wahid, 2024). Malaysia has a structured system for the collecting and distribution of zakat, mostly administered at the state level by several State Islamic Religious Councils (Majlis Agama Islam Negeri, MAIN) (Mıgdad, 2019). These committees guarantee the distribution of Zakat payments to qualified receivers (asnaf), especially the impoverished and destitute (fakir miskin), in alignment with Islamic tenets (Mustafida et al., 2020). Malaysia has several programs running under poverty eradication programs with the help of zakat including direct financial assistance, educational scholarships, entrepreneurship & economic empowerment programs, employment & job placement programs, housing & shelters, and healthcare assistance are some of the prominent programs (Meerangani, 2019). 4. Materials and Methodology In addition to providing the initial capital and necessary resources, the ZPEU project incorporates an ongoing support system for the Asnaf participants. This support system includes regular training sessions and workshops focused on modern and sustainable agricultural practices, financial literacy, and business management. By partnering with agricultural experts, universities, and local agricultural agencies, ZPEU will ensure that participants have access to the latest knowledge and techniques in rice paddy farming. This continuous learning approach aims to enhance the skills and competencies of the Asnaf, enabling them to increase their productivity and yield. Furthermore, mentorship programs are established, where experienced farmers and industry experts will guide and support the participants throughout the project. To ensure the sustainability and scalability of the ZPEU project, a comprehensive monitoring and evaluation framework was developed. This framework involves the collection of both quantitative and qualitative data to assess the project's progress and impact on the Asnaf community. Key performance indicators (KPIs), such as crop yield, income levels, and participants' overall well-being, are tracked and analyzed. Regular feedback sessions are conducted with the participants to identify any challenges or areas for improvement. Additionally, the project also explores opportunities for market linkages and value-added activities, such as branding and packaging the rice, to enhance its marketability and profitability. By continuously refining the project based on data-driven insights, ZPEU aims to create a replicable model that can be expanded to other regions and contribute to the broader goal of socio-economic upliftment of the Asnaf community. ZPEU is a project based on the concept of ‘Daripada Asnaf kepada Asnaf,’ covering three districts in Kedah: Alor Setar, Yan, and Kubang Pasu. Participants will be selected from the Asnaf group, the needy, the poor, or the low-income group (B40), who have experience and capability in rice paddy farming. All costs and initial capital, such as the provision of rice seeds, https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Majid et al. (2026) 4 fertilizers, pesticides, planting equipment, ploughing machinery, harvesting machinery, and other necessary tools, will be borne by LZNK. The harvested rice will then be processed into rice grains and redistributed to the Asnaf in Kedah. Further, we applied both qualitative and quantitative methodology in this study. The qualitative part was based on content comparison methodology grounded by system model approach. Following this model we applied “input, process and output” method. Following this method we collected information from secondary data about participants monthly income before joining the program, income after joining the program and seasonal income. 5. Results and Discussion In the first phase, which ran from August 2021 to January 2022, a total of 10 participants from the asnaf, needy, and poor groups were selected to join the ZPEU and work on the Smart Sawah project, covering 28 hectares of paddy fields in Batu 16, Padang Lumat, Yan, Kedah. For the study purpose all participants selected under Smart Sawah project were included in this study with the permission of ansaf board and the participants themselves. They were are fully aware about the purpose of this study. The participants’ output during the first phase was very satisfactory, with an average yield of five to seven tons per hectare (Table 1). LZNK aims for the ZPEU program to develop 89.6 hectares of land in Yan, which will create new employment opportunities for 30 to 40 asnaf. This project has the potential to make a significant impact on the asnaf and the ummah's economy by helping increase the future income of the asnaf. Before participating in the ZPEU program, the participants’ monthly income ranged between RM800.00 and RM1,350.00. After joining the program, their income more than doubled. With varying sizes of land cultivated, the highest average monthly income earned by participants was RM3,463.20. The highest seasonal income reached RM20,779.20, resulting from 2.78 hectares of land. Meanwhile, the second phase, implemented in 2022, involved 22 asnaf from the Yan District as participants in the Smart Sawah Berskala Besar Asnaf (SSBBA) program. The Zon Pembangunan Ekonomi Ummah (ZPEU) project not only empowers the asnaf through paddy estates but also expands this transformative project to create a new economic ecosystem over seven years, from 2018 to 2025. LZNK has reorganized its land assets, totaling 700 acres in Kedah, for the implementation of paddy cultivation estates. Additionally, smart agriculture practices are employed in paddy farming, and livestock farming is also carried out, including duck farming for salted egg production. Fish farming has commenced with an initial stock of 5,000 puyu fish fry and 230 jelawat fish. Additionally, downstream cultivation is being undertaken by three wives of SSBBA participants, growing crops such as eggplant, okra, and bitter gourd. The ZPEU program will also be expanded to establish rice-based factories, including rice mills, rice vermicelli production facilities, and laksa flour mills, among others. At the same time, the area will be developed into satellite farms and agro-tourism sites, featuring the construction of a floating restaurant for the asnaf. All restaurant management will be handled by local asnaf and B40 community members. Furthermore, paddy farmers in Kedah, Malaysia, encounter various issues that profoundly affect their productivity and livelihoods. Recurring inundation and natural calamities frequently ravage paddy fields, resulting in significant agricultural losses. Moreover, pest infestations, including rodents, and diseases such as grain blight diminish yields and undermine rice quality. The ongoing issue of weedy rice, along with elevated production expenses for fertilisers, pesticides, and machinery, imposes further financial burdens on farmers. Restricted access to contemporary agricultural technologies and insufficient water management systems intensify these challenges, impeding effective farming methods. Additionally, socioeconomic limitations, such cultivation on rented land and limited access to finance, hinder farmers' capacity to engage in enhancements. Resolving these difficulties is essential for improving the resilience and sustainability of paddy cultivation in Kedah. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Majid et al. (2026) 5 5.1. The Selection Process for SSBBA Participants by LZNK Determining the eligible asnaf who are entitled to receive zakat is a decree from Allah SWT, as stated in Surah At- Tawbah, verse 60, which means: “Indeed, zakat is only for the poor, the needy, those who administer it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, for freeing those in bondage, for those in debt, for the cause of Allah, and for the wayfarer (the traveler who is cut off from expenses). This is an obligation (that comes) from Allah. And remember, Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise.” (Surah At-Tawbah 9:60). These eight categories of asnaf have been allocated portions of zakat since the time of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) and continue to be recognized today. All zakat institutions in Malaysia adhere to the same distribution concept, involving the eight asnaf categories that have been established. The screening aspect is crucial to ensure that zakat distribution targets the true asnaf and avoids misallocation or giving zakat to those who are not eligible. Imam Shafie R.A. placed great importance on this matter to prevent mistakes, such as distributing zakat to individuals outside the asnaf categories, as outlined in the Quran. Ensuring that only those who are eligible receive their rightful share is the responsibility of those managing the zakat. The selection procedure for SSBBA participants involves two stages. The first stage involves the Imam of the local area. The involvement of local individuals helps expedite and accurately identify the asnaf since locals are more familiar with the community in that locality. The Imam will be appointed as a supervisor and given an allowance by LZNK. After the screening process at the mosque committee level is completed, the list of selected participants will be sent to the management of LZNK. LZNK will then investigate by visiting the homes of the selected participants to gather more detailed information, such as the number of family members, the condition of the house, and the children's education. Following the investigation and interviews, LZNK will announce the final decision regarding the participants selected to join the Smart Sawah Berskala Besar Asnaf (SSBBA) project. 5.2. Selection Criteria for SSBBA Participants by LZNK Several criteria have been set by the LZNK management, such as the participant must be an asnaf who regularly attends the mosque, is often involved in community activities, and has the desire to improve their living standards. The conditions set are as follows: i. Must be a Muslim; ii. Male; iii. Age not exceeding 60 years (exceptions may be made at the discretion of LZNK officers); iv. Physically healthy; v. Household income below the poverty line; vi. Does not own any land; and vii. Has ability and interest in agricultural activities. In the second stage, the selection process will involve the district zakat officer, who will manage the next steps of the procedure. The zakat officer will assess the eligibility based on the applicant's Had Kifayah and evaluate the applicant's inclination toward rice farming, livestock farming, machinery operation, or any one of these activities. Participants are also required to fill out a form to extend their participation in the SSBBA program, which must be endorsed by the Imam based on their performance, such as frequent mosque attendance and involvement in the community. The selection and screening process is crucial to ensure that zakat distribution targets the true asnaf group. In the initial phase, LZNK selected 10 participants from the asnaf (poor and needy) to join the SSBBA program, involving 28 hectares of paddy fields. LZNK also collaborated with Bank Islam to offer interest-free loans of RM5,000 per season through a micro-financing initiative (Bangkit loan) (LZNK, 2023). In addition to rice cultivation based on smart agriculture, livestock farming is also carried out, such as duck farming for the production of salted eggs. Fish farming is also conducted, starting with 5,000 puyu fish fry and 230 jelawat fish. Downstream farming is managed by three wives of SSBBA participants, involving crops such as eggplant, okra, and bitter gourd. Participants are allowed to engage in downstream agriculture and livestock farming during the 120-day waiting period for rice harvesting (Figure 1). 5.3. Issues and Challenges in Participant Selection The zakat management must identify the asnaf who are eligible to receive zakat assistance, and this is the main challenge in the selection process. Zakat institutions place great emphasis on integrity when performing their duties and responsibilities to ensure that the Zakat funds entrusted to them are managed properly. However, some members of the community do not understand the selection process, leading to negative perceptions of zakat management. They view the zakat application process as too complicated and slow, with investigations taking a long time and various procedures that seem burdensome. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Majid et al. Other issues include participants who lack interest and do not show full commitment to implementing the paddy field program. Some participants fail to adhere to the schedule, while others are involved in social problems. Additionally, some participants are not fully prepared to venture into other agricultural activities, such as vegetable farming and downstream crops. Arising from these issues, LZNK needs to be more selective in choosing SSBBA participants to avoid distributing zakat to those who are not eligible or lack the motivation to improve their family’s economic status. 6. Conclusions The selected SSBBA participants are from the asnaf (poor and needy) group, intending to transform their lives into successful farmers. Participants are given at least two seasons in the program. The recruitment and selection of participants is a highly challenging human resource management function, as it determines the quality of workers who will support the goals of ZPEU. In the effort to develop holistic human capital, particularly within the ZPEU program, strong knowledge is essential. The quality of workers not only depends on their level of education but, more importantly, on the experience they have gained in various fields. These skills and experiences will foster individuals with confidence in their chosen fields. In the process of selecting more competent participants, several improvement suggestions need to be implemented, such as broader advertising, more systematic interview sessions, and conducting psychometric tests to assess participants' potential and interest in the program. The following are some suggestions for improvements that LZNK can implement to sustain this program. 7. Implications of the study The present study has many practical and policy implications. This study will help in enhancing zakat management competency, the development of infrastructure and human capital, community involvement in participant selection, and continuous monitoring. For instance, one suggestion for policy improvement that should be considered is to empower the management of zakat institutions in the screening and selection process of the asnaf. This includes specialized training for zakat management in participant eligibility assessment techniques and the use of technology to streamline the selection and monitoring process. Further, the SSBBA program has shown significant results in increasing the income of the asnaf through smart agriculture. Therefore, LZNK should consider expanding the infrastructure for modern agricultural equipment and establishing its own rice processing plant. Training and related courses should be conducted to produce competent farmers. This includes motivation programs, financial management education, and appropriate skills training to ensure participants can be self- sufficient after the program ends. The SSBBA participant selection process involves the local imam and mosque management, highlighting the importance of community involvement. Therefore, the involvement of the imam and mosque management is highly relevant for selecting qualified participants, as they are more familiar with the participants involved. Moreover, to ensure the success of a program, there must be a continuous monitoring and evaluation system. This is crucial in helping to improve participant efficiency. Moreover, the use of accurate indicators can assist in assessing the effectiveness of the program. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Majid et al. (2026) 7 8. Limitations This research has some shortcomings that need acknowledgement. Initially, its conclusions pertain only to the Smart Sawah Berskala Besar Asnaf (SSBBA) program administered by the Kedah State Zakat Board (LZNK), hence limiting generalisability to other zakat-oriented initiatives. Using only qualitative methodology may limit empirical validation, and the limited sample size (10 participants in the first phase and 22 in the subsequent phase) may not adequately reflect the wider Asnaf community. The participant selection method, including local imams and mosque committees, may create prejudice, thus compromising the impartiality of recruiting. The research largely assesses short-term economic advantages, neglecting long-term sustainability and larger economic implications. This study focused only Pedy formers which in future can be extended to fisheries, and palm oil sector which is also a part of government welfare programs. Furthermore, one of the limitation is that under this only men as head of the project was allowed which is reflecting biasness towards females which are occupying a major portion in Agri farming. Finally, external elements such economic policies, environmental changes, and governmental laws are not thoroughly examined, which may impact the efficacy of the SSBBA program. JSON: Name: ssbba_selection_evaluation Title: Mixed-method quasi-experimental evaluation of participant selection criteria for zakat-funded smart agriculture programs to improve income and retention among asnaf in Kedah, Malaysia Short Hypothesis: Applying selection criteria that require regular mosque attendance, documented community engagement, absence of land ownership, and demonstrated agricultural aptitude causes larger increases in participants' seasonal income and higher program retention over two cultivation seasons compared with selection procedures that do not require these criteria. Related Work: Prior work on zakat-funded interventions and agricultural empowerment has focused primarily on (a) direct cash transfers or capital assistance to asnaf and (b) program evaluations emphasizing short-term poverty metrics. Existing approaches to participant selection typically rely on local referrals (imams, mosque committees) and categorical eligibility (asnaf designation) without rigorous comparative evaluation. Limitations in the literature include small case-study samples, lack of counterfactuals or randomized/quasi-experimental designs, narrow outcome measures (income only), limited assessment of selection-criteria contribution (no ablation of individual criteria), gender and selection biases (male-focused projects), and weak external validity beyond single-district implementations. There is a gap in causal evidence that isolates which specific selection criteria causally improve economic and retention outcomes and how selection design interacts with training, inputs, and market linkages. Abstract: Selection mechanisms used by zakat institutions to enroll asnaf into agricultural empowerment programs are rarely evaluated for causal effect on participant outcomes. This study proposes a mixed-method, quasi-experimental evaluation to test whether LZNK’s current selection criteria (regular mosque attendance, community involvement, lack of land ownership, and agricultural aptitude) produce greater income gains and higher retention than alternative selection rules. We will combine administrative program records, household surveys, plot-level yield data, and qualitative interviews across multiple districts to estimate treatment effects using difference-in-differences, propensity-score methods, and ablation comparisons that remove individual criteria. The main contribution is quantifying the causal contribution of each selection criterion to income, yield, adoption of smart-agriculture practices, and participant retention, producing actionable effect sizes for policy. Expected outcomes include ranked criteria by impact, identification of heterogeneity by gender and plot size, and a validated evaluation protocol for scalable, evidence-based selection in zakat-funded empowerment programs. Experiments: Datasets: (1) LZNK administrative records (applicant screening forms, selection decisions, training attendance, input allocation) for 2018–2025; (2) household surveys at baseline and endline (income, demographics, wellbeing indices); (3) plot-level agronomic records (ha, yield tons/ha per season, input usage); (4) remote-sensing/field-verified cropping data; (5) qualitative interview transcripts. Experimental design: cluster-randomized or quasi-experimental assignment at village/mosque level where possible; target sample size N_total = 240 participants across 3 arms (current LZNK criteria, alternative community-nominated selection, randomized eligible selection), with additional ablation arms that sequentially omit single criteria (n≈60 per ablation condition) for a combined sample target ≈360 observations. Baselines: (A) current LZNK selection procedure; (B) random allocation among eligible asnaf; (C) community-nominated selection without formal criteria. Ablation studies: remove each of the four core criteria individually (mosque attendance, community involvement, landlessness, agricultural aptitude) and measure marginal impact. Evaluation metrics: primary — seasonal income change (RM), retention rate (participation across two seasons), yield (tons/ha); secondary — adoption index of recommended practices (0–1), household wellbeing composite (consumption and food security), loan repayment rate, time-to-adoption. Statistical methods: difference-in-differences with covariates, OLS/GLM for continuous outcomes, logistic regression for retention, instrumental-variable analysis if selection endogeneity detected, propensity-score matching as robustness check. Significance: two-sided tests at alpha=0.05 with cluster-robust SEs. Power: design to detect 20% mean income difference with 80% power. Missing data: multiple imputation. Robustness checks: heterogeneous effects by gender, plot size, prior income; placebo tests on pre-treatment trends. Risk Factors and Limitations: Limited sample sizes and low statistical power if enrollment below targets; selection contamination between clusters (information or inputs shared across groups); measurement error in self-reported income and recall bias; administrative data incompleteness or inconsistent recordkeeping; environmental shocks (floods, pests, weather) creating outcome noise and confounding; non-random program rollout limiting causal identification where randomization is infeasible; persistent gender bias because current program primarily enrolls men, limiting generalizability to women; cultural or political resistance to randomized assignment undermining implementation; external policy or market changes during study period affecting incomes; scalability limits if effects depend on high-intensity support (costly inputs, training) that are not replicable elsewhere; ecological validity constrained to Kedah paddy-rice systems and zakat-funded institutions, reducing transferability to other crops, regions, or non-zakat programs.
